title: Segmented home lab + hardened Linux server
objective: Build a small, documented, reproducible network (firewall + Linux server + attacker VM), harden the server against a benchmark, and prove the improvement with your own audit script.
skills: Virtualization, network segmentation, firewall rules, Linux administration, SSH hardening, Bash scripting, benchmark-driven hardening, technical documentation.
tools: VirtualBox/VMware, OPNsense or pfSense, Ubuntu Server, Kali, nftables/ufw, Nmap, Lynis, ShellCheck, draw.io.
plan: Design the topology and IP plan; draw it before building it.
Deploy the firewall with LAN/DMZ segments; write each rule with a one-line justification.
Deploy the Ubuntu server; enable only the services it needs.
Write audit.sh: UID-0 accounts, SUID files, world-writable paths, listening ports, SSH configuration, sudoers, updates.
Apply a CIS Benchmark subset; re-run the audit; capture before/after.
Scan from Kali with Nmap; explain every open port; close what should not be there.
deliverables: Repository with: topology diagram, IP plan, firewall ruleset with rationale, audit.sh, before/after audit output, Nmap reports, rebuild instructions.
presentation: README opens with the diagram and a two-sentence purpose; a “Findings” section listing what the audit caught and how you fixed it; a “Rebuild in 20 minutes” section.
pitch: “I built a segmented lab and wrote an audit script that checks the eight controls I most often see missing. Hardening cut my own findings from 14 to 3 — and I can show why the last three are accepted risks.”
bar: Basic: screenshots of VMs. Impressive: justified rules, a measurable before/after, accepted-risk reasoning, and instructions that let a stranger rebuild it.

title: Network traffic investigation casebook
objective: Analyze three real capture files and answer, with evidence, what happened, when, and what the defender should do next.
skills: Protocol analysis, Wireshark filtering, indicator extraction, evidence-based writing, the habit of separating observation from inference.
tools: Wireshark, tcpdump, Zeek (optional), CyberChef, VirusTotal (hashes only).
plan: Pick three cases of rising difficulty (a scan, a malware infection, an exfiltration).
For each: build a timeline first, then answer who/what/when/how.
Extract indicators and classify them on the Pyramid of Pain.
Write one page per case: summary, timeline, evidence (filters and packet numbers), indicators, recommendations.
Add a “what I got wrong first” section — it shows method, and senior reviewers read it.
deliverables: Three case write-ups + a reusable Wireshark filter cheat sheet + the indicator list.
presentation: One markdown file per case with screenshots of the decisive packets; the cheat sheet as the repository’s front page.
pitch: “Give me a capture and I will give you a timeline, the indicators and a recommendation — here are three I have already done.”
bar: Basic: answering the quiz questions. Impressive: a timeline, explicit fact-versus-inference language, and recommendations tied to detections.

title: Python security toolkit
objective: Ship a small, tested command-line toolkit that does real work: parse logs, enrich indicators, and triage a Windows host.
skills: Python engineering (structure, tests, packaging), API usage with rate limiting and caching, secrets hygiene, Docker, PowerShell interop, README writing.
tools: Python, pytest, requests, argparse, Docker, gitleaks, VirusTotal/AbuseIPDB APIs, PowerShell.
plan: logparse: auth/web logs → structured records → summary of anomalies (brute force, rare user agents, unusual hours).
enrich: IPs/hashes/domains → reputation data, with caching, rate limiting and offline mode.
wintriage.ps1: processes, services, tasks, connections, recent logons → JSON consumed by the Python tools.
Tests for every parser with fixture files; a --json output mode so tools compose.
Dockerfile, pre-commit with gitleaks, GitHub Actions running the tests.
deliverables: Repository with three tools, ≥ 10 tests, CI badge, Dockerfile, sample data and documented usage.
presentation: README with a 30-second demo (asciinema or GIF), example commands and real output. Issues and pull requests used like a real project.
pitch: “I automate the parts of triage I was repeating by hand — and I test the parsers, because a silent parsing bug is worse than no tool.”
bar: Basic: a 50-line script. Impressive: tests, composability, caching, error handling, CI — the difference between a script and a tool.

title: Enterprise-in-a-box: scripted Active Directory lab
objective: Build a realistic small-enterprise Active Directory environment that can be rebuilt from scripts and instrumented for detection — the environment every later project uses.
skills: Windows Server, AD DS design, GPOs, service accounts, PowerShell automation, logging configuration, lab documentation.
tools: Windows Server, Windows 11 Enterprise, PowerShell, BadBlood or your own population script, Sysmon, GPMC, BloodHound CE, PingCastle.
plan: Design: domain name, OU structure, groups, three realistic departments, one service account with an SPN.
Automate the build (unattended install + PowerShell for OUs, users, groups, GPOs).
Add deliberate, documented weaknesses (weak service-account password, over-privileged group, unconstrained delegation).
Instrument: audit policy, Sysmon with a maintained configuration, log forwarding to the future SIEM.
Baseline with PingCastle and BloodHound; record the attack paths before any attack.
deliverables: Build scripts, environment documentation, deliberate-weakness register, baseline BloodHound/PingCastle reports.
presentation: README with the domain diagram, a “build in one command” section, and the weakness register explaining why each weakness is realistic.
pitch: “I built the environment I then attacked and defended. I can show the attack paths before and after remediation.”
bar: Basic: a domain controller and a client. Impressive: scripted, instrumented, documented weaknesses, and a measurable security posture that improves in P07/P08.

title: Build–break–fix web application
objective: Write a small web application correctly, then break it deliberately, then fix it — and show the diffs. This is the project that proves you understand vulnerabilities rather than recognizing them.
skills: Secure coding (authN/authZ, input handling, password storage, session management), exploitation, remediation, regression testing, threat modeling (extended in M17).
tools: Flask/Express/Next.js, PostgreSQL, Burp Suite, pytest/Playwright, Docker, Semgrep (from M17).
plan: Build the baseline app (registration, login, roles, a resource users can own) with security done properly.
Branch vulnerable: introduce IDOR, stored XSS and a SQL injection — each in a realistic way, not a toy.
Exploit each one with Burp and record proof.
Fix each on main and write a regression test that fails on the vulnerable branch.
Write the comparison: root cause, exploit, fix, test, and the design change that would have prevented it.
deliverables: Two branches, three documented vulnerabilities with exploits and fixes, regression tests, a short threat model.
presentation: README table: vulnerability | root cause | exploit | fix commit | test. Links to the diffs — that table is what reviewers read.
pitch: “I can show you the commit that introduced an IDOR, the request that exploits it, the fix, and the test that keeps it dead.”
bar: Basic: deploying a vulnerable app someone else wrote. Impressive: your own code, your own bugs, your own tests, and a design-level lesson per bug.

title: SOC-in-a-box
objective: Run a miniature security operations centre: collect telemetry from your lab, detect ten techniques, and triage alerts with documented verdicts.
skills: SIEM deployment and tuning, log source onboarding, query writing, ATT&CK mapping, alert triage, playbook writing, case documentation.
tools: Wazuh or Elastic Security, Sysmon, auditd, firewall logs, MITRE ATT&CK Navigator, CyberChef.
plan: Deploy the SIEM; onboard Windows (Sysmon), Linux (auditd) and firewall logs; verify parsing on real events.
Write ten detections mapped to ATT&CK techniques you can actually trigger.
Trigger each one; capture the alert and the underlying evidence.
Write triage playbooks for three alert types (suspicious PowerShell, new service, phishing report).
Triage 25 alerts and write verdicts with reasoning and next actions.
deliverables: SIEM configuration in the repository, detection list with ATT&CK mapping and test evidence, playbooks, 25 triage notes, a coverage layer.
presentation: README with an architecture diagram, a detections table (technique, data source, logic, test result, false-positive notes) and two full sample investigations.
pitch: “I built the pipeline, wrote the detections, tested that they fire, and triaged the alerts they produced — including the ones that were noise, which I then tuned.”
bar: Basic: a screenshot of a dashboard. Impressive: tested detections, false-positive analysis, playbooks and written investigations.

title: Internal penetration test & remediation plan
objective: Run a full engagement against your own Active Directory lab and produce a client-grade report with a risk-based remediation plan.
skills: Methodology, enumeration, exploitation, privilege escalation, lateral movement, evidence handling, CVSS 4.0 scoring, executive communication.
tools: Kali, Nmap, NetExec, BloodHound, Impacket, hashcat, linPEAS/winPEAS, Greenbone/Nessus Essentials, Nuclei.
plan: Write the scope and rules of engagement for yourself — practising the discipline that keeps testers out of trouble.
Enumerate methodically; keep engagement notes with timestamps and commands.
Exploit, escalate and pivot to domain compromise; capture proof at every step.
Score findings (CVSS 4.0) and prioritize using exploitability, asset value, KEV and EPSS.
Write the report: executive summary, methodology, findings with evidence and fixes, strategic recommendations, appendix.
Retest after remediating three findings and document the delta.
deliverables: PDF report (10–20 pages), engagement notes, remediation plan with owners and deadlines, retest results.
presentation: Publish the report as a PDF in the repository plus a README summarizing the attack path in five steps with a diagram.
pitch: “Here is a report I would be comfortable handing to a client: an executive summary a manager can act on and findings an engineer can fix.”
bar: Basic: a list of tool outputs. Impressive: a narrative attack path, business-relevant risk framing, prioritized remediation and a retest.

title: Detection-as-code repository
objective: Turn attacker behaviour into tested, versioned detections with continuous integration — and prove coverage with real test results.
skills: Sigma authoring, purple teaming, false-positive tuning, CI for detections, coverage measurement, incident reporting.
tools: Sigma + pySigma/sigconverter, Atomic Red Team, your SIEM from P06, GitHub Actions, ATT&CK Navigator, Velociraptor.
plan: Choose 15 techniques you can execute safely in your lab (from P07 and Atomic Red Team).
Write a Sigma rule per technique with a documented detection strategy (data source, logic, known gaps, expected false positives).
Execute each atomic test; record whether the rule fired and tune until signal beats noise.
Add CI that validates rule syntax and converts rules to your SIEM query language.
Produce an ATT&CK Navigator layer from test results, not intentions.
Run one simulated intrusion end to end and write the incident report.
deliverables: Rules repository with tests, CI pipeline, coverage layer, tuning notes, one full incident report.
presentation: README explaining the detection lifecycle you follow, with one exemplary rule documented end to end (hypothesis → logic → test → tuning → result).
pitch: “Every rule in this repository has a test that proves it fires and notes on what it misses. I measure coverage from test results, not from wishful mapping.”
bar: Basic: a folder of copied Sigma rules. Impressive: your own rules, executed tests, honest gaps, CI, and an incident report that uses them.

title: GRC pack for a fictional SME
objective: Produce the documents a small company actually needs: a risk assessment, a framework gap analysis, three policies and an executive summary.
skills: Risk assessment method, NIST CSF 2.0 profiles, CIS Controls, ISO 27001 structure, policy writing, executive communication.
tools: Spreadsheets, NIST SP 800-30, CIS Controls v8.1, CSF 2.0 quick-start guides, draw.io.
plan: Define the fictional company precisely (size, sector, systems, cloud usage, regulatory exposure) — vagueness ruins GRC work.
Inventory assets and data flows; identify threats and vulnerabilities.
Build the risk register: likelihood, impact, inherent and residual risk, owner, treatment.
Run a CSF 2.0 / CIS IG1 gap assessment and produce a 90-day prioritized roadmap.
Write three policies people can follow, with defined exceptions.
Write a one-page executive summary that a non-technical director could act on.
deliverables: Risk register, gap assessment, remediation roadmap, three policies, executive summary, optional tabletop exercise report.
presentation: A clean repository or PDF pack; the executive summary first, everything else as annexes — exactly how it would be delivered to a client.
pitch: “I can translate technical findings into a risk register and a 90-day plan that a director will approve, and I can defend each rating.”
bar: Basic: a copied policy template. Impressive: a specific company context, defensible ratings, costed priorities, and a plan tied to real controls.

title: Cloud attack → detect → respond lab
objective: Deploy a deliberately vulnerable cloud environment as code, exploit it, detect every step, respond to the incident, and ship the hardened version.
skills: Cloud IAM, Terraform, cloud attack paths, CloudTrail/GuardDuty detection engineering, cloud incident response, posture management.
tools: AWS, Terraform, AWS CLI, Pacu, Prowler, CloudTrail/Athena, GuardDuty, IAM Access Analyzer.
plan: Terraform an environment with realistic flaws: an SSRF-able app on an instance with metadata v1, an over-permissive role, a bucket with sensitive data, missing logging.
Exploit the chain: SSRF → instance credentials → data access → privilege escalation. Record every API call.
Build detections for each step and validate by replaying the attack.
Run the response playbook: revoke sessions, rotate keys, scope the exposure, write the incident report.
Harden as code (IMDSv2, least privilege, bucket policy, logging, SCP/RCP) and re-run the attack to prove it fails.
Run Prowler before and after and publish the score difference. Destroy everything; keep the costs near zero.
deliverables: Terraform for vulnerable and hardened states, attack walkthrough, detection rules, incident report, Prowler before/after.
presentation: README as a story: architecture → attack path diagram → what the logs showed → response → fixes → proof it now fails.
pitch: “I can show the CloudTrail events for each step of a cloud compromise, the detections that catch them, and the Terraform change that stops it.”
bar: Basic: completing CloudGoat scenarios. Impressive: your own environment, full attack–detect–respond–fix loop, and measurable posture improvement.

title: DFIR investigation report
objective: Investigate a compromised host from disk and memory evidence and produce a report that answers what happened, how, when, and what to do now.
skills: Evidence handling, Windows artifact analysis, memory forensics, timeline construction, disciplined reporting.
tools: FTK Imager, KAPE, Eric Zimmerman tools, Volatility 3, Plaso, Timeline Explorer, Autopsy.
plan: Choose a public case image or generate your own by attacking a snapshotted VM.
Acquire and hash the evidence; document the chain of custody.
Triage: execution artifacts, persistence, account activity, network traces.
Memory: processes, injected code, network connections, credential artifacts.
Build the timeline; separate what the evidence shows from what you infer.
Write the report: executive summary, scope, timeline, findings with evidence, IOCs, containment and hardening recommendations.
deliverables: Investigation report, timeline (CSV/Timeline Explorer), IOC list, the commands used (so results are reproducible).
presentation: Report as PDF plus a README with the timeline highlights and the three artifacts that cracked the case.
pitch: “Given a host and an alert, I can produce a defensible timeline and tell you what to contain first — here is one I did end to end.”
bar: Basic: answering lab questions. Impressive: reproducible methodology, explicit uncertainty, and recommendations that a responder could act on tonight.

title: Threat intelligence report → detection package
objective: Turn open-source reporting about one adversary or campaign into an analytical product and into working detections.
skills: Intelligence lifecycle, source evaluation, ATT&CK mapping, confidence language, detection derivation, stakeholder-focused writing.
tools: ATT&CK Navigator, MISP or OpenCTI, abuse.ch feeds, your SIEM, Sigma.
plan: Pick a campaign with several independent public reports; state the intelligence requirement you are answering.
Extract TTPs and map them to ATT&CK, citing the source sentence for each mapping.
Write the assessment with calibrated language (“likely”, “high confidence”) and explicit gaps.
Derive five detections and test them in your lab; note which TTPs cannot be detected with your telemetry.
Add a one-paragraph executive brief and a defender action list.
deliverables: Intelligence report (5–8 pages), ATT&CK layer, five tested detections, hunting queries, TLP marking.
presentation: README stating the requirement, the key judgments, and the detections — CTI that ends in detections is what employers actually want.
pitch: “I read the reporting, mapped the behaviours, then proved which of them I could actually detect with the telemetry I had.”
bar: Basic: summarizing a vendor blog. Impressive: multi-source analysis, calibrated confidence, explicit collection gaps, and tested detections.

title: Malware analysis report + YARA rules
objective: Analyze two commodity samples safely and convert the findings into detections others can use.
skills: Safe lab handling, static and dynamic analysis, PE structure, deobfuscation, YARA authoring, IOC extraction.
tools: FLARE-VM, REMnux, PEStudio, capa, FLOSS, Ghidra, x64dbg, Procmon, FakeNet-NG, YARA, CyberChef.
plan: Verify lab isolation before touching a sample (no host-only leakage, snapshots ready).
Static triage: hashes, imports, strings, packing, capa capabilities.
Dynamic: file/registry/network behaviour, persistence, C2 patterns.
Light reverse engineering of one interesting function in Ghidra.
Write YARA rules; test against the samples and against a clean corpus for false positives.
Map behaviours to ATT&CK and write two Sigma detections.
deliverables: Two analysis reports, IOC lists, tested YARA rules, Sigma detections, ATT&CK mapping.
presentation: Reports in the repository with a clear safety notice, hashes only (never the samples), and the rules ready to reuse.
pitch: “I triage a sample in two hours and leave the team with indicators, YARA rules and detections — not just a sandbox link.”
bar: Basic: pasting a sandbox report. Impressive: your own static/dynamic evidence, tested rules with false-positive analysis, and detections.

title: Secure delivery pipeline: commit → signed image → hardened Kubernetes
objective: Build the pipeline that prevents the vulnerabilities you learned to exploit, and deploy to a cluster that resists the attacks you learned to run.
skills: Threat modeling, secure code review, SAST/SCA/secret/IaC scanning, SBOM and signing, policy as code, Kubernetes hardening, runtime detection.
tools: GitHub Actions, Semgrep, Trivy, Syft/Grype, gitleaks, Checkov, ZAP, cosign, kind, Kyverno, Falco, kube-bench.
plan: Threat model the application (DFD + STRIDE) and map mitigations to ASVS requirements.
Pipeline stage 1: lint, unit tests, Semgrep (including 5 custom rules), gitleaks.
Stage 2: dependency scanning, SBOM generation, container build with a minimal non-root image, image scan.
Stage 3: sign the image and verify the signature at deploy time; fail closed.
Stage 4: deploy to a hardened kind cluster (least-privilege RBAC, NetworkPolicies, restricted Pod Security Standard, Kyverno policies).
Stage 5: runtime detection with Falco; prove three attack scenarios are caught.
Document the exception process — a pipeline nobody can bypass legitimately is a pipeline teams will route around.
deliverables: Repository with pipeline definitions, custom rules, SBOM, signing and verification, cluster manifests, Falco rules, threat model, exception policy.
presentation: README with a pipeline diagram, a table of each gate and what it blocks, and screenshots of a blocked build and a caught runtime attack.
pitch: “I built the paved road: a commit with a hard-coded secret or a vulnerable dependency does not reach the cluster, and if something malicious runs anyway, Falco catches it.”
bar: Basic: adding a scanner to a workflow file. Impressive: threat-model-driven gates, custom rules, provenance, admission control, runtime detection and a usable exception path.

title: LLM application red-team & hardening
objective: Build a realistic AI application with tools and retrieval, attack it systematically, harden it, and measure the improvement.
skills: LLM application architecture, prompt injection (direct and indirect), tool and agent abuse, guardrail design, evaluation methodology, AI security reporting.
tools: Python, an LLM API or Ollama, a vector store, garak, PyRIT, promptfoo, Burp Suite, Docker.
plan: Build a support assistant: retrieval over documents you control + two tools (a read tool and an action tool).
Threat model it with OWASP LLM/Agentic Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS; mark trust boundaries.
Attack: direct injection, indirect injection via a poisoned document, system-prompt extraction, tool misuse, data exfiltration through rendered output, memory poisoning.
Measure each attack over ≥ 10 runs and record the success rate.
Harden: scope tools per user, enforce authorization outside the model, isolate retrieved content, encode output, allow-list egress, add approval gates.
Re-measure; add the attack suite to CI so regressions are caught.
deliverables: Application repository, attack case library with reproducible prompts, before/after metrics, hardening notes, red-team report.
presentation: README with the architecture, the trifecta analysis (data, untrusted content, egress), a metrics table and the residual risks named honestly.
pitch: “I reduced the success rate of indirect prompt injection from 80% to under 10% by removing the agent’s ability to exfiltrate, not by writing a better system prompt — and I can show the numbers.”
bar: Basic: screenshots of a chatbot saying something silly. Impressive: reproducible attacks, measured rates, architectural mitigations and honest residual risk.

title: AI-augmented analyst assistant with an evaluation harness
objective: Build an AI assistant for your own track workflow — and, more importantly, prove with data how good it is and where it fails.
skills: Applied AI engineering, evaluation design, ground-truth datasets, metrics, cost analysis, failure taxonomy, human-in-the-loop design.
tools: Python, an LLM API and/or a local model, promptfoo or a pytest harness, your own data from P06–P14.
plan: Choose the task by track: alert triage, recon summarization, cloud finding explanation, code review support, agent testing, control mapping.
Build a ground-truth dataset of ≥ 100 items from your own labs (never client or personal data).
Build the assistant with structured output so results can be scored automatically.
Evaluate: accuracy/precision/recall, cost per item, latency, and a taxonomy of failures.
Iterate on prompts, context and guardrails; keep a changelog of what actually moved the numbers.
Add a human-in-the-loop design: what it may do alone, what needs review, what it must never do.
deliverables: Repository with the assistant, dataset, evaluation harness, results table, failure analysis and an operating policy.
presentation: README leading with the results table and the failure taxonomy — the evaluation is the project; the assistant is the excuse.
pitch: “My assistant agreed with my verdicts on 84% of 120 historical alerts, and I can describe the 19 cases where it was confidently wrong and why.”
bar: Basic: a chatbot wrapper. Impressive: a ground-truth dataset, measured results, an honest failure analysis and an operating policy — this is what AI-augmented work looks like professionally.
